name: StrongMinds
summary: StrongMinds runs six-week group talk therapy (interpersonal psychotherapy) for depression, mostly for adolescents and adult women in Uganda and Zambia, increasingly through government volunteers and peer facilitators. This models its 2025 work, the latest year with audited accounts: 745,224 people treated at about $15 each including overhead. It comes to about 3.2 years of healthy life per $1,000. The biggest uncertainty is how large and lasting the effect is at scale: the one randomised trial of StrongMinds' own delivery found an effect a third the size of the wider literature's, gone within two years, so the model weights the two equally.

rows.label: Total expenses (all programs, management, fundraising), 2025

source.title: StrongMinds, Inc. and related entities, combined financial statements for the years ended December 31, 2025 and 2024 (audited; auditor's report dated June 25, 2026)

rows.explainer: Total combined expenses for 2025 from the same statement: program services 7,316,320, general and administrative 3,115,986, fundraising 958,047.

rows.label: Spending on the depression-therapy programme, 2025
rows.explainer: All of 2025's program spending: StrongMinds' one programme, group interpersonal therapy in Uganda, Zambia and through partners in Ethiopia, Kenya, Malawi and Nigeria (the US entity's own program spending after eliminations, $744,703, combining schedule p.21, pays for the partner countries and technical staff). StrongMinds America, the only other programme, ceased on December 31, 2024 (note 1), so nothing is taken out. Psychoeducation and sensitisation sessions are how clients are mobilised and screened into groups, so their cost is part of the cost of each client treated.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ program expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programs in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do. StrongMinds' general and administrative costs are high (27% of total expenses in 2025), so this multiplier, 1.56, matters.

People treated for depression in 2025

source.title: StrongMinds, Q4 2025 report
source.page: p.2 (and the CEO letter, p.4: 'reaching 745,224 people with depression in 2025'; p.1's 754,224 is a typo)

rows.explainer: StrongMinds' own count of clients who received its six-week group interpersonal therapy (IPT-G) in 2025, up from 426,642 in 2024: delivered by its staff, by government volunteers, by NGO partners and by peer facilitators (former clients, Zambia). Not independently verified; how far the count overstates people who got the therapy as studied is in implementation_adj.

rows.label: Share of clients in Uganda, 2025
rows.explainer: StrongMinds hasn't published 2025 clients by country. Anchor: in 2024 Uganda treated 236,292 of 426,642 clients, 55% (Q4 2025 report, p.6); high end 72%, Uganda's share of the two African entities' 2025 program spending (4,703,501 of 6,571,617, combining schedule, printed p.21), which overstates it because Zambia's peer-led groups cost less per client. The rest are in Zambia and the partner countries, whose household sizes (rural Kenya 4.2, rural Malawi 4.3, Nigeria 4.5) are close to Zambia's 4.7. Used only to weight household size and the suicide rate.

rows.label: Cost per person treated
rows.explainer: Context: StrongMinds reports $15 per person for 2025 (Q4 2025 report) and $23 for 2024; this is total spending over clients, the same.

rows.label: Effect of psychotherapy for adult depression in non-Western countries, trials at low risk of bias (SD)

source.title: Cuijpers et al. (2018), Psychotherapies for depression in low- and middle-income countries: a meta-analysis, World Psychiatry 17(1):90-101

rows.explainer: The meta-analytic prior: Hedges' g at the end of treatment for psychotherapies for adult depression in non-Western countries (mostly low- and middle-income; 8 of 32 comparisons in high-income places such as Taiwan; few in Africa), restricted to the six trials at low risk of bias. All 35 comparisons give 1.10, 0.73 after adjusting for publication bias, and low/lower-middle-income countries 0.83; the low-risk-of-bias trials, 0.51, are the better guess for what a well-run programme does, since the larger effects come from weaker trials and care-as-usual controls. Group formats did as well as individual ones (0.94 vs 0.89).

rows.label: Effect of StrongMinds' therapy in its own RCT, end of treatment (PHQ-8 points, among attenders)

source.title: Baird, Özler, Dell'Aira, Parisotto and Us-Salam (2024), Therapy, Mental Health, and Human Capital Accumulation among Adolescents in Uganda, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10849 (published in the Journal of Development Economics 176, 2025)
source.page: Table A4 (LATE), Panel A, PHQ-8 score: -0.730 (SE 0.552)

rows.explainer: The one randomised trial of StrongMinds' own delivery: IPT-G by StrongMinds Uganda for adolescent girls (13–19, PHQ-8 ≥ 10) in BRAC clubs around Kampala, 2019. The effect on the PHQ-8 among those who attended at least one session (instrumented, so comparable with StrongMinds' count of clients treated) was 0.73 points lower right after therapy (95% CI −0.35 to 1.81, the range), 0.58 at 12 months and none at 24. PHQ-8 is the PHQ-9 without the self-harm item, on nearly the same scale.

rows.label: Effect in StrongMinds' RCT, in SDs
rows.explainer: PHQ points into standard deviations by the site's one spread of PHQ-9 scores among people starting therapy (@depression.phq9_sd, 4.21); the trial's own control SD was 4.82.

rows.label: Weight on StrongMinds' own RCT against the meta-analytic prior
rows.explainer: How much the charity-specific trial counts against the literature. Reference class, a precision-weighted blend: the trial's 0.173 SD has a standard error of 0.131 (0.552 / 4.21); the prior's 0.51 has 0.09 from its interval, which alone would give the trial 0.0081 / (0.0081 + 0.0172) = 32%; but predicting a new implementer needs the prior's between-study spread too (I² = 60% across the six trials, τ² about 0.03–0.06), which raises the trial's weight to about 65–80%. Down from there: the trial is unrepresentative of 2025's programme in ways that make it pessimistic. The authors call it 'a first attempt by StrongMinds to provide IPT-G to adolescents and to work through partner organizations'; therapy ended months before COVID-19; attendance was low (28% attended 12 of 14 sessions); and StrongMinds has since changed the adolescent model (teachers instead of peer mentors, in-school groups). Up: it is StrongMinds' own delivery in Uganda, and adolescents are a large share of clients (about 267,000 of 745,000 in 2025, 36%, on the likeliest reading of the Q4 2025 report's chart). Two differences cut the other way, and are counted in evidence_adj, not here: the trial gave 14 sessions where the 2025 model gives six, and the trial's groups were run by StrongMinds' own trained facilitators, while only 3% of 2025's clients were treated by StrongMinds staff (the rest by government volunteers, NGO partners and peers). Best 50%, range 30–75%.

rows.label: Effect at the end of treatment (standard deviations), blended
rows.explainer: The prior and StrongMinds' trial, weighted. StrongMinds' own pre–post figure, a 12.1-point fall on the PHQ-9 two weeks after therapy (Q4 2024 and 2025 reports), has no control group: in the RCT the control group's PHQ-8 also fell from about 13 at baseline to 8–9, so most of a pre–post change is recovery that would have happened anyway. It is not used.

rows.label: Years until the effect has faded

source.title: Baird, Özler, Dell'Aira, Parisotto and Us-Salam (2024), Therapy, Mental Health, and Human Capital Accumulation among Adolescents in Uganda, World Bank Policy Research Working Paper 10849 (published in the Journal of Development Economics 176, 2025)
source.page: Table A4 (LATE), PHQ-8 score: -0.730 at the end of therapy, -0.578 at 12 months, +0.192 at 24 months

rows.explainer: From StrongMinds' trial, per attender (the same basis as the effect): 0.73 PHQ-8 points at the end of therapy, 0.58 at 12 months and gone at 24. That area, 0.5 × (0.73 + 0.58) + 0.5 × 0.58 = 0.945 point-years, is a linear fade from 0.73 over 0.945 / (0.5 × 0.73) = 2.6 years. The intention-to-treat estimates (Table 6: 0.354, 0.404, none) look flat in the first year only because more of the people reached at 12 months had attended therapy (0.354 / 0.730 = 49% at the end of therapy, 0.404 / 0.578 = 70% at 12 months), which the per-attender estimate corrects for. StrongMinds' own 12-month before-and-after follow-ups are not used: no control group, and heavy attrition. Low 1.5: a fade complete by about 18 months. High 4: about two-thirds of 2025's clients are adults, and the adult trial in rural Uganda (Bass et al. 2006, British Journal of Psychiatry 188:567–573) found the effect undiminished six months after therapy; adults may keep gains longer than adolescents hit by COVID-19 (the 12-month round was a phone survey during lockdown).

rows.label: Implied decay of the effect (SDs per year)
rows.explainer: Context: compare with the decay in StrongMinds' trial (about a fifth of the effect in the first year among attenders, the rest in the second).

rows.label: Discount rate, continuous
rows.explainer: The shared yearly rate as a continuous rate, so the effect can be discounted smoothly as it fades.

rows.label: Discount factor for the fading effect
rows.formula: if(continuous_discount_rate > 0, (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years - 1 + exp(-(continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years))) / (0.5 * (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years) * (continuous_discount_rate * effect_duration_years)), 1)
rows.explainer: Present value of the triangle (linear fade to zero) at the shared rate, as a share of its undiscounted area; as in the HLI models.

rows.label: Total effect per person (SD-years, discounted)
rows.explainer: Area of the triangle: linear decay from the initial effect to zero, discounted.

rows.label: WELLBYs per person treated
rows.explainer: SD-years into WELLBYs at the site's one rate (@wellby_factors). The WELLBY slider then puts WELLBYs into healthy years, calibrated so a year of depression is worth the same here as through the GBD weights (@depression); never convert depression into DALYs inside this model.

rows.label: Household size (Uganda and Zambia, weighted by clients)
rows.explainer: The site's household size for each place (facts/household_size.json: Uganda 4.7, 2024 Malaria Indicator Survey; Zambia 4.7, 2024 DHS), weighted by where the clients were treated.

rows.label: Household multiplier (recipient plus spillovers)
rows.explainer: Each other household member gains the site's one share of the recipient's effect (HLI's, @wellby_factors).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), a multiplier
rows.explainer: What the blended effect still leaves out. External validity: the 2025 programme is a six-session group therapy run at scale by government volunteers, teachers and peers with light supervision, shorter than the 8–16 sessions of most trials, so some dilution is likely (×0.85). Internal validity: even the low-risk-of-bias trials measure depression by self-report, open to social-desirability bias in therapy groups (×0.9). Together 0.75 (0.5–0.95). Check against StrongMinds' own RCT: after all adjustments (total_adj, 0.54) the effect counted is about 0.18 SD per client, 1.1 times the trial's 0.17 SD among attenders at the end of therapy; the blend already gives the trial half the weight, so this is not a second discount for the same evidence.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The effect sizes are already net of their control groups, which had care as usual (22 of 32 comparisons in Cuijpers et al.; the trial's controls the same local access as anyone), so the treatment people would have had anyway is already taken out. 1, with a low of 95% in case StrongMinds' scaled channels now reach people who would otherwise have been treated by the growing government services.

rows.label: StrongMinds' share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Others' resources, in dollars against StrongMinds' own $11.39 million (total expenses). Uganda's and Zambia's governments each covered about 9% of 2025 program costs (Q4 2025 report, p.6; 97% of it government staff time recruiting, training and supervising the volunteer facilitators, plus transport stipends and space): 0.09 / 0.91 × $6.57 million of the two countries' program spending ≈ $0.65 million. Kenya's counties (7–19%) and Malawi's government (about 10%) on the much smaller partner-country programmes: about $0.05 million. NGO partners, who treated 21% of 2025's clients (about 156,000) with their own staff (StrongMinds' 'Partners' expense fell to $39 in 2025): a judged $3–10 of their own cost per client, between the governments' in-kind $0.89–3.69 per patient (p.6) and StrongMinds' own program cost of $9.82 per client (7.32 million / 745,224), so about $1 million (0.5–1.6). Volunteer and peer facilitators, who ran about three-quarters of the groups (some 566,000 clients), give time beyond their stipends: a judged 2 hours per client at a rural wage of a few tens of cents an hour, about $0.4 million (0.2–0.8). Together about $2.1 million: 11.39 / (11.39 + 2.1) = 0.84. Low 0.78: partners at $1.6 million and volunteers at $0.8 million (others $3.1 million); high 0.94: governments only.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: The client count is StrongMinds' own administrative figure and isn't independently verified; it tripled in two years (239,672 in 2023, 745,224 in 2025), mostly through government channels whose groups StrongMinds supervises less closely, and the count's definition (started or completed) is not published. The effect used is per person who attended at least one session (the RCT's LATE) or enrolled (the meta-analysis), so completion is already in it; this is for clients counted who didn't get therapy as studied. 85%, range 65–100%.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

rows.label: Female suicide deaths per 100,000 a year, Uganda, 2021

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Suicide mortality rate, female (per 100,000 female population), SH.STA.SUIC.FE.P5 (WHO Global Health Estimates)

rows.explainer: The female population's suicide rate (the both-sex rate is 5.5: men account for most suicides), the base the excess risk of people with depression is applied to. Most clients are women and girls; school groups include some boys, whose higher rate this leaves out.

rows.label: Female suicide deaths per 100,000 a year, Zambia, 2021

source.title: World Bank, World Development Indicators: Suicide mortality rate, female (per 100,000 female population), SH.STA.SUIC.FE.P5 (WHO Global Health Estimates)

rows.explainer: Zambia's female rate (both sexes 7.13), used for the clients outside Uganda.

rows.label: Female suicide deaths per 100,000 a year, weighted by clients
Relative risk of suicide with major depressive disorder

source.title: Moitra et al. (2021), Estimating the risk of suicide associated with mental disorders: a systematic review and meta-regression analysis, Journal of Psychiatric Research 137:242-249
source.quote: predicted adjusted RRs ranging from 4·11 [2·09, 8·09] for dysthymia to 7·64 [4·3, 13·58] for major depressive disorder

rows.explainer: How much more likely people with major depression are to die by suicide than the general population, from the meta-regression the Global Burden of Disease uses. Clients are screened in by a PHQ cut-off rather than diagnosed, so some have milder depression (dysthymia's 4.11 is near the low end).

rows.label: Share of depression's excess suicide risk removed while the effect lasts
rows.explainer: No trial of group therapy in Africa is large enough to measure suicides. Anchor: the effect here, about 0.34 SD before adjustments, is a fraction of the gap between depressed and non-depressed people on the PHQ-9 (roughly 2–3 SD), so it removes perhaps a sixth of the excess risk while it lasts (15%). Low 3%: depression's link to suicide is partly through causes therapy doesn't touch. High 40%: StrongMinds screens for suicidal thoughts and refers clients (formal protocols since 2025).

rows.label: Suicides averted per person treated (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Excess suicide risk of a depressed client (the female rate × (relative risk − 1)) × the share removed, over the years the effect lasts with the effect fading linearly (× 0.5), discounted like the fading effect (discount_factor). About one suicide averted per 30,000 people treated.

rows.label: Value of a death averted (units of value)
rows.explainer: GiveWell's moral weight for a death at 15–49 (StrongMinds' clients are adolescents aged 15–24 and adult women), times your value of a life.

rows.label: Deaths averted, in units of value
Deaths averted, in WELLBYs (cancelled by the unit's conversion)
rows.explainer: The one row that puts units of value into WELLBYs; the WELLBY unit's conversion multiplies it back, so the deaths count exactly their shared value at any WELLBY rate.
